Stories / Constantinople · Vienna · France · 1547–1548

Story · Habsburgs, France and the Ottomans, 16th century

Constantinople, 1547: Henri II’s letters to Suleiman, copied by Ferdinand’s spy

In the summer of 1547, Charles V and his brother Ferdinand have just concluded the Truce of Adrianople with Suleiman. Henri II, king for a few months, sends one of his pantlers, the sieur d’Huyson, to Constantinople with letters for the Sultan. The letters do not stay secret: Ferdinand’s resident at the Porte, Giovanni Maria Malvezzi, obtains their text, puts it into Latin and sends it to his master in cipher. Read today, his four pages show what the King of France really wrote to the Sultan, and what the Habsburgs knew of it.

Story by Brice Dudout · reading with Claude · Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue, no. 500 · document: Österreichisches Staatsarchiv, HHStA, Türkei I 7-2-18 · published 14 November 2026

« non uenerunt sincere causa agiendi pacem, sed potius decipiendi »

“They did not come sincerely to treat of peace, but rather to deceive”: Henri II to Suleiman, on the envoys of Charles V and Ferdinand, Türkei I 7-2-18, f. 143v (cipher passage).

What is new, what was known

Known. D’Huyson’s mission has been known since the seventeenth century. In 1666 Jean Ribier printed, in French, Henri II’s letter of credence to the “Grand Seigneur” and the instruction given to d’Huyson; in 1850 Ernest Charrière published the letters from Venice and Constantinople that follow his journey.[1] Malvezzi’s cipher alphabet was found, with a letter of Ferdinand I of January 1548, in the DECODE database, and read by Daniel Bourdeau.[3]

What we add, to our knowledge. (1) The text of the Vienna item, which the archive’s inventory still describes today as “nicht dechiffriert” (not deciphered): read, about 97% of the groups.[2] (2) The Latin text of the letters as it circulated at the Porte, which is not a translation of Ribier’s French. (3) Two notes by Malvezzi on the way the French present their letters to the Sultan. (4) A third letter, on the Diet of Augsburg, the Ottoman fleet and Barbary, of which we found no equivalent in Ribier or Charrière.

1547: a truce that isolates France

By 1547 the war for Hungary has lasted twenty years. Suleiman has held Buda since 1541; Ferdinand of Habsburg, King of Hungary and brother of Charles V, keeps only the north and west. In June 1547, at Adrianople, the two brothers’ envoys sign a five-year truce with the Sultan: Ferdinand recognises Ottoman rule and pays each year 30,000 gold florins for what he keeps.[4] For Charles V, who has just crushed the Protestant princes at Mühlberg (24 April 1547), it means peace in the East just as he gathers at Augsburg the Diet that is to bring the Empire to heel.

For France it is a danger. Since Francis I, the alliance with the Sultan has been the weapon that forces the Habsburgs to fight on two fronts. Francis I dies on 31 March 1547; his son Henri II inherits a truce negotiated partly behind his back, and the ambassador his father had sent to the Porte, Gabriel de Luetz, seigneur d’Aramon.

The king’s pantler

The king then sends one of his ordinary pantlers, the sieur d’Huyson, to Constantinople. He passes through Venice in early September 1547, sails in October, falls gravely ill in Constantinople and does not leave until the end of January 1548; he is back in Venice at the end of March, with a “cappitaine Bartholomeo”.[1] His instruction, printed by Ribier, has two faces. Outwardly the king adheres to the truce and asks that his allies be included in general terms, “& specialement les treize cantons des ligues des Suisses, & les deux de la ligue grise”. But if the imperial ratification is slow in coming, d’Huyson “parlera autre langage”: all that the Emperor and the King of the Romans have done was only to gain time.

This double language was known only from the instruction given to the envoy. The Vienna item shows what was written to the Sultan himself.

A spy at the Porte

Giovanni Maria Malvezzi represents Ferdinand in Constantinople. On 8 March 1548 he encloses with a despatch an annex “A” of four pages entirely in cipher: the copy of the letters brought by d’Huyson.[2] Between two letters he explains, in Italian, where his text comes from. The French, he writes, do not present the king’s letters at the Porte as the Most Christian King wrote them: they have them put into Turkish language and script, adding and cutting as they please, with neither date nor place, “a chautela loro per posser negare”, as a precaution, so as to be able to deny them. “Io cauo queste scritture dal turchesche in latino de uerbo ad uerbum”: he himself draws these writings from the Turkish into Latin, word for word.

The Latin of the item is therefore a back-translation from the Turkish, which explains its irregular syntax: it is the text the Ottoman chancery had before it, not the French draft. How did Malvezzi get the Turkish version? He does not say; access to someone close to the Ottoman chancery is the simplest hypothesis. A second note introduces the last letter, carried “doppo Dussun” by “un certo capitano”: probably Charrière’s Captain Bartolomeo.

What the king writes to the Sultan

The credence (15 lines) accredits “istum nobilem […] credencerium nomine Duson”, this nobleman, the pantler named Duson, who will come with the ambassador “Gabriele de Ramon” on business “that must be told by word of mouth”: he is to be believed “tanquam praesentialiter affuissem”, as if the king were there in person. It is the formula of Ribier’s French text, but drafted “in the Turkish manner”, with the Ottoman titles and “mi frater carissime”, my dearest brother.

The second letter is an indictment of the truce. The king recalls that his father had obtained a one-year truce for the envoys of Charles V and Ferdinand, and that they then came back to treat a five-year peace “without the knowledge” of the late king. His ambassador at the imperial court has obtained, “with remarkable diligence and skill”, copies of the letters of ratification; d’Huyson brings them to the Sultan. In them, says the king, the fraud is plain: the Emperor did not swear, “as is the custom of emperors or kings”; he slipped “at the end” articles from the old Treaty of Crépy (1544), counting on the Porte having no interpreters to understand them; had he really wanted peace, he would have sent princes. The king asks that the peace be held firm only if the Emperor includes France in it “with its friends and confederates”, first of all the Swiss, from whom he draws his armies. And he slips in an argument about money: those who promised thirty thousand florins for a few places in Hungary would have given a hundred thousand; with those places they can “recover the whole kingdom of Hungary”; on the contrary, they must remain “weak on all sides”.

The third letter turns to war. The King of Spain, “a man who knows much, but a deceiver”, has gathered the princes of Germany “in ciuitate Augusta” (the Diet of Augsburg) and asked them for help, an army and money: “day and night they are ready for any occasion of war”. Let the Sultan keep his fleet ready and send his captains to the king’s aid; if the Spaniards attack Barbary, the king will send his fleet with the Ottoman armada. The letter finally confirms d’Aramon as ambassador.

These letters change the light on the mission. Officially, Henri II adhered to the truce; to the Sultan, he asks him to hold it void if his allies are not included, not to leave Hungary to the Habsburgs, and to arm his fleet. And Ferdinand knew this as early as March 1548, through his resident.

The texts and their reading →

The cipher

  • An alphabet of signs: numerals, Greek letters, invented shapes; a family of “8”s is told apart by the foot (e, d, r, x).
  • A few homophones and double values (4 = dd).
  • Nulls: the syllables Dam, Dem, Dim, Dom, Dum and dotted signs.

It is the alphabet Malvezzi shared with Ferdinand: DECODE keeps the table with Ferdinand’s letter to Malvezzi of 23 January 1548, which Daniel Bourdeau read.[3]

How we read it

  1. A frozen key. The DECODE alphabet was calibrated on another ciphered copy in the same file (7-3-20), which carries its contemporary decipherment, then fixed by a SHA-256 fingerprint before any reading of 7-2-18.
  2. A blind test. On an unglossed copy of a ciphered letter of 1550 (8-3-8), the decoding was frozen before the contemporary decipherment was opened: 92.5% of letters agree (84.3% from the key alone), against 20% on average and 31% at most for permuted keys.
  3. A sign-by-sign reading of the 207 lines, on the archive’s full-resolution images, with no known text. On 145v the ink of the recto shows through: we subtracted it digitally to read.
  4. Brice Dudout’s blind review: twenty doubtful signs, shown as shapes with no reading visible, on two sheets; nineteen confirmed, one re-examined and kept.
  5. Ribier and Charrière were used only to identify people and check the sense, never to fix a value.

What remains uncertain

  • The count. 1,146 groups were counted one by one: 1,124 read, i.e. 98.1%. The other 404 or so (143r l. 18 – 143v l. 16, 145v ll. 28–30 and 146r) were estimated line by line, at around 95%. In all, about 97.4% of some 1,550 groups; even at 90% for the estimated part, the item would stay above 95%. Eighteen groups remain unresolved, four of them in the Italian heading.
  • A second-hand text. The Latin is Malvezzi’s back-translation of a Turkish version which, he says, the French had themselves retouched. It should not be credited with the precision of a royal draft.
  • Dates. The credence is of summer 1547; the second letter is later than the imperial ratification, the third later than the opening of the Diet of Augsburg (September 1547). None is dated in the copy, as Malvezzi points out.
  • Prior work. Checked on 14 November 2026: the archive’s inventory, Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue and repository, a web search. The volume Austro-Turcica 1541–1552 (1995), which edits other items of this series, was not consulted; the inventory records no edition of this one.
  • No images. The images can be seen on the Austrian archive’s online inventory; they are not reproduced here.
